en: Eulogy for the Venerable Dazhi of Lingzhi Monastery in Qiantang (with Preface),
composed by the disciples Yanxiang, Lianruo, and Ze’an.
Following the peaceful passing of the Venerable Dazhi, whom they had previously served, a fellow student requested that they compose a eulogy for his anniversary.

For many years I have lacked the leisure [to compose this]. Suddenly, one night, I dreamed that I entered a room where several practitioners were discussing the life and noble deeds of our former master.

His understanding and practice were peerless. As they spoke, one said slowly, "To support the collapsing and sustain the precarious, thereby establishing teachings for the world—his merit is not inferior to that of the various patriarchs.
Why do you, sir, not compose a eulogy? Upon waking, I happened to obtain several couplets, and thus...

I have compiled these fragments into a composition, hoping it may be comparable to folk songs. Yet, in honoring the end and commemorating the distant past, it lies in the intent and not in the literary form;

thus, I am truly without shame. (Upon entering the ritual hall, after performing the three prostrations, the participants kneel alternately while burning incense and scattering flowers. Holding hand-incense burners, they chant:)
I prostrate to the Great Wisdom Vinaya Master, the Founder of the Lingzhi School. His enlightened nature was clear from his youth, and his reputation for learning spread far and wide.

He profoundly penetrated the subtle mysteries of Buddha-wisdom, and his pure cultivation perfectly accorded with the sacred rites. He strictly observed the regulations of the Single Character (Ekākṣara) and was fully capable of upholding the trust of the "Hundred Gold" (the imperial succession).
Inheriting the profound Dharma, he served as the Crown Prince of Zhongnan, establishing two altars that endure through all eternity.

He compiled the Three Records (*Sanji*), transforming the *Feng* and *Ya* odes and manifesting the ultimate teaching. With celestial eloquence, he discoursed upon the eternal truth, grandly extolling the Supreme Vehicle (*Shangsheng*).

He fathomed the ancestral source to realize the ultimate reality (*shi*). Thus, when his mission in Jambudvīpa was complete, he sought out the destruction of the seals [of the Dharma] and departed for the East.
His merit in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing was perfected; suddenly, his writings were completed and he departed toward the West.

Now, as the early autumn begins and the anniversary of his passing approaches, I have thus ventured to utter these crude words to further proclaim his flourishing achievements. With the sense that his disciplined body is still present, I shall reverently offer these sacrificial gifts with solemnity and decorum.

The Dharma words are difficult to encounter; we can only endure our lamentations and shed tears of blood. We look up with hope that you will graciously turn your compassionate gaze toward us to briefly accept this expression of sorrowful sincerity.

May you deign to allow those who carry their books upon bamboo frames to all be included within the ranks of those who share the lamp of wisdom. (Having finished chanting, they prostrate once, rise, and kneel again while holding the incense burner to make the request.)
With single-minded devotion, we respectfully invite the Great Wisdom Vinaya Master, the Founder of the Lingzhi School.
We pray only that you will descend to this ritual site and accept our offerings. (Recite three times; after one prostration, rise and offer this praise:)
Fully endowed with majestic dignity, his physical marks correspond to his mind; his resolute and lofty spirit corresponds to his marks.
To speak of him as square when he is round—whether constrained or released, he neither clings nor transgresses;
thus gods and humans turn toward him in devotion.
(After the eulogy, recite the memorial verses. Alternatively, state your specific intentions as the occasion requires; compose these yourself. Then, perform the prostrations and praises, chanting:
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Venerable Lingzhi, who attained renown at the Great Monastery, abandoned his home to enter the Way, and manifested his physical body at that time.
The net of craving is tenuous; he contemplates severing its bonds. Familiar with the paths of the monastic gardens, he recognizes their winding turns.
Compared to a neighbor’s child who warns his parents, he points and looks about, startling the temple deities and the vast assembly.
With hair tied in youth, he already displayed ancestral refinement at the brush; reaching the age of maturity, he topped the examination halls in the study of the scriptures.
In the school hall, he dipped his brush; his spirit was such that it could swallow an ox. As my ancestral master, I shall instead show him reverence;
therefore, with a single mind, I take refuge in him and prostrate myself before him. (The following are all modeled after this).
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the ancient Buddhas’ path: the body that enters the marketplace to beg for food;
a single bowl held at the crossroads, the mind likened to the moon. Where the two rings sway, the will soars above the clouds;
passing through crimson gates for the noon meal, one stays far removed from wrong seeking and maintains pure livelihood entirely.
The portion taken is no different from the offerings of the Gandhavatī Buddha; presented here, it resembles the milk-rice of a cowherd.
Freshly divided and shared even with insects and fish, may I, through shame and compassion, equally bestow this Dharma-gift.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to the one who possesses both Sūtra and Vinaya, and whose eloquent speech flows like a hanging river at the opportune moment.
Long ago you made a pact at Vulture Peak, receiving the Master’s personal entrustment; Heaven ordained the Patriarchal Master to exhort you to turn your heart back [to the Dharma].
The wind rises from the elephant-fan, the cypress smoke floats upward; Clouds gather around the lion throne as fourfold flowers rain down.
Striking your shoulder, you restored the true realm; Clapping your hands in approval, you probed the profound mysteries of the Great Sūtra.
In Pingfen, the Vinaya-tiger’s claws and fangs were perfected; at the Cave of Yu, the Righteous Dragon sighed over the prostrate deer.
With single-minded devotion, he paid homage to those who propagated and clarified the practice, and while secluding himself behind closed doors, he composed this record for his own lifetime.
The Great Dharma is gentle and yielding, truly attained within; this culture flows forth as the brush sweeps across the silk.
You maintain the vast net of the world and rectify the collapsing cords, riding side-by-side with the Five Vehicles back to the true track.
Like Confucius, you have exhausted the three types of bamboo slips to seek out the hidden; like the sages of old, you have sought the four seals of the ink to probe the profound depths.
Dozing upon a tuft of *túfú* grass, I dream of Ximing Monastery; More than sixty households have become moth-eaten scrolls.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate before those in the depths of the water-and-clouds retreat, Who strike away my ignorance so that my present body may receive further growth.
From afar I admire the traces of the Sage during his days in Jingzhao; I loftily follow the profound model at the time on the banks of the Cai River.
Once again I augment the superior grade of the path to Nirvana; Fully endowed with the three causes, I aspire to liberation.
Mountains and rivers surge forth as fellow practitioners from the Brahma world arrive; The void dissolves and perishes as the celestial Māras are moved.
The holy embryo and the Dharma-milk depend upon this person; though one were to grind one's bones and shatter one's body, it would be difficult to repay such virtue.

With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to the one who dwells in the hidden, true, and secluded hermitage by the emerald pond, whose physical form is currently engaged in expounding the commentaries.
Shaking out my robes, I gradually approach the temple by the water’s edge; Treading my sandals, I ascend the green peaks and ridges.
A single stone and long pines satisfy my simple heart; Morning monkeys and night cranes watch over my deep meditation.
Filtering spring water, the evening pond is as blue as lapis lazuli; Opening the scroll in the autumn hall, the *campaka* flowers are fragrant.
The lost texts of the Grand One, the wind of the primordial antiquity— after fifteen hundred years,
one meets a connoisseur who bows with single-minded devotion to the body of the Master who built the altar at Mount Tai and the Yin River to bestow the precepts.
The five-colored peaks rise beneath Mount Jin; The three-tiered peaks stand abruptly amidst the ridges.
Like pearls, they are round and bright, shining like the sun and stars; Their celestial forms are solemn and manifest, suspended like a balanced mirror.
The sacred model accords with the Dharma as the capital city does its provinces; The precious formations pierce the clouds like Mount Wutai.
The one who further illuminates the *Vinaya* appears once more; from afar in the void, I imagine seeing you, Piṇḍola, as I pay homage with single-minded devotion.
I prostrate myself with a solemn oath to benefit all beings, so that this single flower shall remain unmoving for the duration of your lifespan.
I have traveled through famous monasteries seeking stillness, finding joy in dwelling at sublime temples amidst lakes and mountains.
Contemplating the deep fragility of this body like a flame or a phantom, I linger here, letting others laugh at my gourd-like traces.
Having departed from India—the land of a hundred years of disputes—I now bid farewell to the dusty realm, the slope of chrysanthemums, as if it were but a single dream.
During a great drought, he delivered the *Mahāmegha Sūtra* at Chaoyin Monastery; before the banquet had even ended, rain fell from the sky.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to his physical body as he sat cross-legged in meditation at Qiaogao Lansi to manifest his parinirvāṇa.
With head turned north, he drew his arms across his chest to gaze at the setting sun; as the westward light receded, he recognized the path of his return.
Startled, he rose and immediately sat in the full lotus posture; with a sudden gasp, he passed away, then slowly closed his eyes.
His spirit traveled clearly as he entered deep meditative absorption; his head remained raised high, appearing as if he were still alive.
The residents of the village lanes remained unaware in their silence;

they heard only the celestial music resounding through the void as they prostrated with single-minded devotion before the stupa containing the remains of the Blessed One at the auspicious site of Jeta Grove.
On this day of solemn rites at the Lotus Society, amidst the bitter cold, The pine boughs are scorched and curled, yet they defy the frost.
Mist pours from the four eaves while the candles remain bright; A thousand apertures howl with wind, yet the incense does not fade.
Great waters freeze into ice like jeweled steps; The vast sky stirs snow as if flowers are falling.
With crowns, canopies, banners, and streamers, we mourn the Crane Forest; the names inscribed upon it are exquisite, and his radiant legacy remains.
With single-minded devotion, we pay homage at the stupa where auspicious signs appeared, and where the burning of the scriptures failed to destroy his physical body.
For a long time the *Brahmalakṣaṇa-sūtra* was upheld in meditative concentration; the stupa stood firm in Zhizhu Garden, revered for its eternal preservation.
Though bandits and fire raged fiercely until nothing remained, the sturdy pillar remained utterly unaltered by even the slightest change.
Dragons and devas provided protection, manifesting auspicious omens; nobles and commoners alike gazed upon it with reverence, sighing in wonder at such an extraordinary encounter.
After passing away, he left behind his physical form for the benefit of those with karmic affinity; during his life, he aided all beings—how could one calculate such merit?
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to the One of Purple Majesty who cherishes the Way; at the time of his posthumous enfeoffment and commemoration, his very person was honored.
The era of Zhenghe has passed for six years; in the autumn of the tenth year of Shaoxing, his excellence was honored.
How could his descendants not enjoy the wind of compassion? Though he is aged, he can still recount the traces of his transformation.
For several decades, reports of his life have been heard, leading to the rites of posthumous title and honor. From the Nine Palaces, a bounty has descended, bestowing upon him a grand name.
His great wisdom is as vast as the ocean, equal to that of the Buddha; The radiance of his precepts shines brilliantly throughout the realms of sand.
With a sincere heart, he repents for and establishes the three thousand essential prohibitions; He expounds upon the eighty thousand rules of dignified conduct.
Yet though I have been foolish and stubborn, failing to restrain my mind, I now resolve to be as solemn as the Shu-shen people, deeply guarding against the mind’s following after delusions.
Where appearances and emptiness are difficult to discern, The convergence of karma and causes ensures that fruits do not fail to manifest.
Facing the compassionate light with reverence, I repent for all my transgressions, Hoping that, like the brilliant sun, they may melt away like frost and snow.
Having completed the repentance, take refuge with the utmost sincerity and pay homage with the crown of the head.
With the utmost sincerity, make this vow:
throughout immeasurable kalpas in this world and other realms, whether among humans or in the heavens, may I always be together with my Teacher.
Using wisdom, one can board the boat of Prajñā; Through physical supernormal powers, one reaches the shore of Bodhi.
Firmly and perfectly cultivating the three clusters of precepts, Resolutely never retreating from the Four Great Vows.
All those who are enemies or kin throughout the past, present, and future lives— Are fully transformed so that all return together to the Land of Peaceful Nurturing.
Having made this vow, I take refuge with a sincere heart and prostrate in worship.
The hymn of praise composed by Xiang of the Right Cliff precedes the title "Xixiao" (錫號), yet it lacks the appellation "Dazhi" (大智).

It is appropriate that these be specially added. Furthermore, the "Celestial Palace" (Tiāngōng) has been changed to "Numinous Mushroom" (Língzhī), so that all may understand the beauty of the enshrinement and posthumous title of the stupa, which represents the final manifestation of his extraordinary signs.

Since the eulogy was previously missing, two additional chapters have been appended at the end, so that the narrative may be complete from beginning to end. Among these, there are certain expressions that remain somewhat unsatisfactory.
I have occasionally revised certain characters; this does no harm to the underlying principle.

Having observed that Master Dazhi of the Vinaya School made numerous additions and alterations to the liturgical texts across various editions, I venture to follow his precedent in commissioning the carving of these woodblocks.
May they reach my fellow followers of the same lineage, so that on the anniversary of the [Master’s] passing, they may rely upon them to perform the rites of honoring their ancestors.
The Text of Liturgical Praise Composed by the Vinaya Master Dazhi (Xingxun), Resident of Mingqing Monastery,
on the Mid-Autumn Day of the Jiazi Year of the Xiangxing Era (concluded).
